preamble: In the process of Tonogenesis, the debuccalization of a final sibilant [s] into a glottal fricative [h] represents a critical intermediate stage. According to Haudricourt's model, this Laryngeal Coda originally triggered a lowering of the vowel's Pitch Contour, which eventually became phonemicized as a falling tone (Qù sheng or sắc/nặng).
phoneticEffects: Debuccalization, Tonogenesis, Pitch Fall, Voice Loss, Falling Tone

examples.note: Historical final -s in Mon-Khmer was first debuccalized to -h and then elided, giving rise to the 'Sắc' (high-falling) tone in Vietnamese.
A primary stage in Haudricourt's model where final sibilants weakened to laryngeal fricatives.
The 'Departing' category (Qù sheng) in Middle Chinese is reconstructed as having a final [s] (later [h]) which influenced the Pitch Contour of the syllable.
Led to the development of the Qù (去) or Departing tone.
Tai-Kadai languages show a similar pattern where final spirants debuccalized, contributing to the development of the falling tone register.

One of the most significant phonetic innovations distinguishing Guarani from Tupi is the systematic replacement of sibilant /s/ with glottal fricative /h/. E.g., Proto-Tupi *so → Guarani ha (color), *se → Guarani he (this), *sipo → Guarani hipo (snake). This represents a regular sound law in the Tupi-Guarani divergence, not driven by tonogenesis but by debuccalization of the anterior fricative.

One of the most diagnostic Iranian sound laws: Proto-Indo-Iranian word-initial *s → Proto-Iranian *h before vowels. Classic example: PII *sapta 'seven' → Avestan hapta, Persian هفت haft. Sanskrit preserves *s: saptá. Similarly PII *sṷana- 'dog' → Avestan spā (via *h-), Old Persian *ha-. The change was blocked before non-nasal stops and after i, u, r, k.
PII *s → Iranian *h word-initially. Compare Sanskrit sūra- 'sun' which preserves *s. This isogloss defines the Iranian branch of Indo-Iranian alongside the satem-like sibilant shifts.

In Buryat, the inherited sibilant *s debuccalized to /h/ before vowels other than *i. E.g., Proto-Mongolic *sang 'storehouse' → Buryat han(g); *sira 'yellow' → Buryat shara (via intermediate *h-palatalization). The change is blocked before *i, where *s is preserved or merges with palatal outcomes. This parallels the spirantization of *c→s in the same language.
Regular initial *s- > h- before vowels in Brythonic; cf. Irish sean
Lenition of s, grammaticalized only in Goidelic
Eastern Polynesian *s > h; Samoan keeps sina
